ety.text: From Middle English lesarde, lisarde, from Anglo-Norman lusard, from Old French lesard (compare French lézard), from Latin lacertus, which is of obscure origin. Displaced native Middle English aske, from Old English āþexe (> modern English ask, askard).

senses.d: Any reptile of the order Squamata that is not a snake or mosasaur—typically characterised by a rounded torso, a short neck with an elevated head, a long tail and four limbs, although some species are legless.
ex: The forms of the serpent and lizard exhibit almost every element of beauty and horror in strange combination; […]
Hooded rattlesnakes, horned toads, and lizards crawl in the dust and among the rocks.

senses.d: Lizard skin, the skin of these reptiles.
ex: Silver bells jingling from your black lizard boots, my baby / Silver foil to trim your wedding gown

senses.d: A hand forming a "D" shape with the tips of the thumb and index finger touching (a handshape resembling a lizard), that beats paper and Spock and loses to rock and scissors in rock-paper-scissors-lizard-Spock.
A person who idly spends time in a specified place, especially a promiscuous woman.
ex: lounge lizard; lot lizard; beach lizard; truck stop lizard

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French lezart, from Old French lezart, lesard, laisarde, lajjsarde, from Latin lacertus. Compare English lizard.
From Latin lacertula, diminutive of lacerta (“lizard”). Doublet of alligatore. Compare Galician, Spanish, and Portuguese lagarto (“lizard”).
Inherited from Old Spanish lagarto, from Vulgar Latin *lacartum, from Latin lacertus.

Inherited from Old Spanish lagartixa, equivalent to lagarto + -ija. Probably from a Vulgar Latin *lacarticula, diminutive of *lacartum. Compare Portuguese lagartixa, Asturian llagartesa, Catalan llangardaix.

pt:lagarto.gl: wall lizard (reptile of the family Lacertidae)

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese lagarto, from Vulgar Latin *lacartum, from Latin lacertus, of uncertain origin.
